    Critical SharePoint RCE flaw exploited to steal machine keys
    bleepingcomputer.com · 21 Jul 2026 20:06 UTC openai-codex / gpt-5.5
    TAGSbinaryformatter-deserializationcve-2026-50522defusedgithubmachine-key-theftmicrosoftmicrosoft-sharepointpowershellsecuritycontexttokenwatchtowrws-federation
    In plain words

    Hackers are using a serious flaw in Microsoft SharePoint to break into vulnerable company-run SharePoint servers, and working example code for the flaw is now public. The people affected are organizations that run their own SharePoint systems and have not fully dealt with the issue. This matters because attackers can steal special server keys that let them pretend to be real users and open SharePoint sites and documents with those users’ access, even after the software is patched.

    Summary
    Hackers are actively exploiting the critical Microsoft SharePoint RCE flaw CVE-2026-50522 to steal machine keys, letting them forge authentication tokens and maintain access even after patching. Organizations should apply Microsoft’s July updates and rotate exposed credentials or keys on affected SharePoint servers.

    Hackers are actively exploiting the critical CVE-2026-50522 vulnerability in Microsoft SharePoint against vulnerable on-premise deployments. Microsoft describes the issue as a deserialization-of-untrusted-data flaw that allows a remote attacker to execute code over a network without authentication. The flaw was addressed in Microsoft’s July security updates, but it was not marked as actively exploited at the time.

    watchTowr reported that exploitation attempts began shortly after proof-of-concept exploit code became public, with its honeypot network capturing attempts that successfully compromised target systems. The attackers are stealing machine keys, which can allow them to create valid authentication tokens, impersonate users, and access SharePoint sites and documents with the forged identity’s privileges. Defused also detected an undocumented SharePoint deserialization vector in attacks as early as July 17 and later said the activity was likely tied to CVE-2026-50522.

    At least one PowerShell demonstrative exploit for CVE-2026-50522 is available on GitHub from security researcher Janggggg. The proof of concept attempts to trigger remote code execution by sending a malicious .NET BinaryFormatter payload as the cookie of a forged SecurityContextToken in a WS-Federation sign-in response to SharePoint’s ‘/_trust/default.aspx’ endpoint. While applying the latest SharePoint security updates removes the vulnerability, watchTowr advises defenders to also rotate credentials on any asset that may have been exposed.

    • Patching alone may not be enough for exposed SharePoint servers because stolen machine keys can let attackers keep forging valid authentication tokens after the vulnerability is fixed.
    • The exploitation timeline was extremely compressed, with watchTowr reporting successful honeypot compromises within hours of identifying public proof-of-concept code.
    • Defused observed related attack activity as early as July 17, before the activity was publicly linked to CVE-2026-50522.
    • The public proof-of-concept targets SharePoint’s WS-Federation sign-in flow by placing a malicious .NET BinaryFormatter payload inside a forged SecurityContextToken cookie.
    Key Points
    • 01Hackers are actively exploiting the critical CVE-2026-50522 vulnerability in Microsoft SharePoint to steal machine keys and maintain access even after affected servers are patched.
    • 02Microsoft describes CVE-2026-50522 as a deserialization-of-untrusted-data flaw that allows a remote attacker to execute code over a network without authentication.
    • 03Microsoft addressed the flaw in its July security updates, and the advisory noted an increased likelihood of exploitation even though it was not marked as actively exploited at the time.
    • 04watchTowr reported that attackers began targeting vulnerable on-premise SharePoint deployments shortly after proof-of-concept exploit code became public.
    • 05At least one PowerShell proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2026-50522 is available on GitHub and attempts to trigger remote code execution through SharePoint’s '/_trust/default.aspx' endpoint.

In plain words

A serious flaw in Microsoft SharePoint Server is being actively used by attackers after public example attack code was released. It affects organizations running on-premises SharePoint Server versions, including Subscription Edition, 2019, and 2016. The issue matters because attackers can use it to run their own code on a company’s SharePoint server, steal secret machine keys that help them keep access, and potentially place harmful software there.

Summary
Microsoft SharePoint Server CVE-2026-50522, a critical remote code execution flaw, is now being actively exploited after a public proof-of-concept was released. Organizations running on-premises SharePoint should patch immediately and rotate exposed machine keys or credentials, because attackers are using the bug to steal keys and maintain persistence.

A third SharePoint Server flaw patched by Microsoft in its July 2026 Patch Tuesday update is now under active exploitation, according to watchTowr. The vulnerability is CVE-2026-50522, a critical deserialization of untrusted data issue in Microsoft Office SharePoint with a CVSS score of 9.8. Microsoft said it could allow an unauthorized attacker to execute code over a network and credited DEVCORE researcher “splitline” with discovering and reporting it.

Microsoft’s advisory said a network-based attacker authenticated as at least a Site Owner could write arbitrary code to inject and execute code remotely on the SharePoint Server. The company also rated exploitation as “Exploitation More Likely.” watchTowr said it observed active exploitation against on-premises Microsoft SharePoint deployments after a public proof-of-concept exploit was released, and said attackers are pulling SharePoint machine keys through a single request.

Defused Cyber said threat actors are likely exploiting CVE-2026-50522 to deliver a .NET deserialization payload to a SharePoint sign-in endpoint, with captured requests carrying no authentication material. The article notes that CVE-2026-50522 is the third SharePoint Server vulnerability after CVE-2026-56164 and CVE-2026-58644 to see active exploitation efforts. CISA has warned that multiple SharePoint Server vulnerabilities are being exploited against supported on-premises versions, including Subscription Edition, 2019, and 2016, to gain unauthorized access and support post-exploitation activity such as IIS machine key theft, persistence, and malware deployment.

  • Patching CVE-2026-50522 alone may not remove the risk from already targeted SharePoint servers, because watchTowr said attackers are stealing machine keys that can support persistent access.
  • The article presents a discrepancy in access requirements: Microsoft’s advisory text says an attacker must be authenticated as at least a Site Owner, while Defused Cyber said captured exploit requests carried no authentication material.
  • CVE-2026-50522 became the third SharePoint Server flaw from the July 2026 patch cycle to face active exploitation, indicating that attackers are repeatedly targeting the same on-premises SharePoint ecosystem.
  • CISA’s warning links the exploited SharePoint flaws not only to initial unauthorized access, but also to follow-on activity such as IIS machine key theft, deserialization techniques, persistence, and malware deployment.
Key Points
  • 01Microsoft patched CVE-2026-50522, a critical deserialization vulnerability in Microsoft Office SharePoint with a CVSS score of 9.8, as part of its July 2026 Patch Tuesday update.
  • 02watchTowr reported active exploitation of CVE-2026-50522 against on-premises Microsoft SharePoint deployments after the release of a public proof-of-concept exploit.
  • 03watchTowr said attackers are using a single request to pull SharePoint machine keys and warned that patching is not enough because exposed credentials should be rotated.
  • 04Defused Cyber said threat actors are likely exploiting CVE-2026-50522 to deliver a .NET deserialization payload to a SharePoint sign-in endpoint without authentication material.
  • 05CISA warned that threat actors are exploiting multiple SharePoint Server vulnerabilities affecting supported on-premises versions, including Subscription Edition, 2019, and 2016, to gain unauthorized access and perform post-exploitation activities.

    In plain words

    Hackers are using serious flaws in WordPress, a widely used website system, to break into vulnerable sites without needing a login. Once inside, they can add hidden access points, install harmful add-ons, collect site administrator names and emails, and even create new administrator accounts. This matters because affected websites can remain under an attacker’s control unless owners update WordPress and check for unwanted files, plugins, or users.

    Summary
    Attackers are actively exploiting critical WordPress Core wp2shell flaws to install malicious plugins, PHP webshells, and rogue admin accounts on vulnerable sites. Administrators should update immediately to the patched WordPress versions and check for signs of compromise.

    Hackers are actively exploiting the critical “wp2shell” vulnerability suite, tracked as CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, affecting WordPress Core. The flaws are being used to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins on affected servers. WordPress addressed the issue in versions 7.0.2, 6.9.5, and 6.8.6, and automatic security updates were forced for supported installations.

    The exploit chain abuses the WordPress REST API’s batch-processing feature, allowing remote attackers to execute code on vulnerable installations without authentication. Wiz reported activity including mass scanning, malicious plugin uploads, PHP webshell installation, collection of administrator usernames and email addresses, local file inclusion attempts targeting wp-config, and successful access to WordPress administration panels. Wiz said it has not observed lateral movement or data exfiltration but continues to monitor the activity.

    Johannes B. Ullrich described two-stage attacks that begin with SQL injection probing before delivering a PHP webshell under the /wp-content/cache/ directory. The webshell used a randomized filename that also functioned as a password and returned a fake 404 page otherwise. Administrators are urged to update immediately, review logs for wp2shell-related requests, inspect installed plugins, and check for rogue PHP files or newly created admin accounts.

    • Some observed scanning activity is from security scanning rather than attackers, so administrators reviewing logs may need to distinguish malicious attempts from benign probes.
    • The webshell described by Johannes B. Ullrich hides behind a fake 404 page unless accessed with the correct randomized filename used as a password, making simple page checks less reliable for finding compromise.
    • Wiz has not observed lateral movement or data exfiltration in the attacks it tracked, indicating the reported activity has so far centered on initial compromise and persistence.
    • Defiant observed exploitation-related probing within minutes of the public timeline, with initial probing at 23:29 UTC on July 17 and a clear SQL injection attempt 13 minutes later.
    • A live dashboard cited in the article estimated an 81.6% patch rate from a sample of 124,580 websites, showing that a meaningful minority of sampled WordPress sites may still remain exposed.
    Key Points
    • 01Hackers are exploiting the critical wp2shell vulnerability suite, CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, affecting WordPress Core to deploy persistent webshells and install malicious plugins on affected servers.
    • 02The exploit chain abuses the WordPress REST API’s batch-processing feature to allow remote code execution on vulnerable WordPress installations without authentication.
    • 03Wiz reported observed activity including mass scanning, malicious plugin uploads, PHP webshell installation, administrator username and email collection, local file inclusion attempts targeting wp-config, and successful access to WordPress administration panels.
    • 04Johannes B. Ullrich described two-stage attacks that probe for SQL injection before delivering a PHP webshell under the /wp-content/cache/ directory with a randomized filename also used as a password.
    • 05Administrators are advised to update to WordPress versions 7.0.2, 6.9.5, or 6.8.6, review logs for wp2shell-related requests, inspect installed plugins, and check for rogue PHP files or newly created admin accounts.

In plain words

Attackers are taking advantage of two serious flaws in WordPress that can let them break into vulnerable websites without needing a username or password. The issue affects default WordPress sites from recent versions, and researchers have already seen widespread scanning, stolen account details, fake administrator accounts, malicious plugins, and hidden control files placed on compromised sites. This matters because many organizations use WordPress, and a compromised website can be fully taken over unless it is fixed and checked for signs of earlier abuse.

Summary
Attackers are actively exploiting the wp2shell WordPress vulnerability chain to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution, create backdoor admin accounts, and deploy malicious plugins or web shells at scale. WordPress site owners should patch immediately and check for compromise even if updates have already been applied.

Attackers have begun exploiting two critical WordPress vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, collectively called wp2shell. When combined, the flaws can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and complete compromise of vulnerable websites. WatchTowr said exploitation was already underway by early Saturday UTC, first using public exploit code to exfiltrate hashed credentials and later moving to remote code execution after more details became public.

The exploit chain was discovered by Searchlight Cyber using OpenAI GPT 5.6 Sol and is described as having no preconditions against a stock WordPress installation with no plugins. Cloudflare said CVE-2026-63030 enables unauthenticated remote code execution only when persistent object cache is not in use, while the SQL injection vulnerability CVE-2026-60137 is present from WordPress 6.8 onward and the remote code execution issue affects versions from 6.9. Intruder said CVE-2026-60137 is an entry point involving a REST API batch endpoint route confusion bug that bypasses authentication.

Wiz observed post-exploitation activity including malicious plugin uploads, user enumeration, harvesting of administrator usernames and email addresses, local file inclusion attempts targeting database credentials and authentication keys, admin panel access, and PHP web shell uploads. Attackers have also used a 150 KB web shell disguised as a WordPress security plugin called CMSmap, and WatchTowr said its honeypots saw tens of thousands of exploitation attempts after a public exploit was released. Defenders are advised to inspect WordPress instances for new administrator accounts, malicious plugins, and suspicious files regardless of whether the sites have been patched.

  • Patched WordPress sites may still require incident response because defenders are advised to check for new administrator accounts, malicious plugins, and suspicious files regardless of whether fixes have already been applied.
  • The remote code execution issue is conditional: Cloudflare said CVE-2026-63030 enables unauthenticated remote code execution only when persistent object cache is not in use.
  • The risk is not limited to customized WordPress deployments because Searchlight Cyber said the exploit chain works against a stock installation with no plugins and no preconditions.
  • Attackers are using fake WordPress plugins as a persistence and execution method, including a 150 KB web shell disguised as a legitimate security plugin called CMSmap.
  • Some observed activity consists of high-volume scanning without follow-on compromise, which Wiz said suggests opportunistic mass scanning alongside legitimate security scanning activity.
Key Points
  • 01Attackers have begun exploiting two critical WordPress vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137, collectively called wp2shell, to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution and compromise vulnerable websites.
  • 02Searchlight Cyber said the exploit chain has no preconditions and can be used by an anonymous user against a stock WordPress installation with no plugins.
  • 03Cloudflare said CVE-2026-63030 enables unauthenticated remote code execution only when persistent object cache is not in use, while CVE-2026-60137 is present from WordPress version 6.8 onwards and the remote code execution issue affects versions from 6.9.
  • 04Wiz observed post-exploitation activity including malicious plugin uploads, user enumeration, harvesting of admin usernames and email addresses, local file inclusion attempts targeting database credentials and authentication keys, admin panel access, and PHP web shell uploads.
  • 05WatchTowr said its honeypots registered tens of thousands of exploitation attempts after a public exploit was released, and more than 100 backdoor administrator accounts were created following exploitation.

In plain words

Attackers are now taking advantage of a serious flaw in ServiceNow AI Platform that can let someone with no login run their own commands on a ServiceNow system. This matters because the flaw could allow a full takeover of a ServiceNow instance and connected proxy servers. ServiceNow has released fixes, and customers using self-hosted versions are being urged to apply them.

Summary
Threat actors are actively exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical pre-authentication sandbox escape flaw in ServiceNow AI Platform that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution and full instance compromise. ServiceNow has released patches, and self-hosted customers should update immediately.

Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-6875, a critical security flaw affecting the ServiceNow AI Platform, according to Defused Cyber. The vulnerability has a CVSS score of 9.5 and is described as a sandbox escape issue. It could allow an unauthenticated user to run arbitrary code.

ServiceNow released patches for the flaw throughout June across Brazil EA and GA, Australia Patch 2, Zurich Patch 7b and Patch 9, and Yokohama Patch 12 Hot Fix 1b and Patch 13. Searchlight Cyber said it reported the issue on April 1, 2026. The firm said the flaw could allow complete compromise of a ServiceNow instance and all connected proxy servers.

Defused Cyber said the observed exploitation targets the pre-authentication endpoint /assessment_thanks.do using HTTP POST requests. The article notes that the sandbox-escape gadget leads to the same code execution primitive by a different route than the one documented in the proof-of-concept exploit. In light of active exploitation, self-hosted ServiceNow customers are advised to apply the fixes if they have not already done so.

  • Defenders can focus monitoring on HTTP POST requests to the pre-authentication endpoint “/assessment_thanks.do,” because Defused Cyber observed active exploitation targeting that endpoint even when the route to code execution differs from the published proof-of-concept.
  • The potential impact extends beyond the ServiceNow instance itself, because Searchlight Cyber said exploitation can also compromise all connected proxy servers.
  • ServiceNow is not only patching the flaw but also restricting what code can run in sandbox contexts, indicating the fix includes broader hardening of the affected execution environment.
  • Self-hosted ServiceNow customers are singled out for urgent patching, making them the most immediately actionable audience in the article.

    In plain words

    A criminal group called Qilin is using a serious weakness in Palo Alto Networks’ GlobalProtect software to get into organizations’ networks without permission and lock up their files for ransom. Palo Alto fixed the issue in May, but unprotected systems are still being targeted, and U.S. officials ordered federal agencies to secure affected systems quickly. This matters because many organizations around the world use Palo Alto products, including major banks and large companies, and Qilin has already claimed more than 2,000 victims.

    Summary
    The Qilin ransomware gang is actively exploiting Palo Alto Networks’ critical PAN-OS GlobalProtect authentication bypass flaw, CVE-2026-0257, to break into networks and deploy ransomware. Organizations with exposed GlobalProtect instances should patch or mitigate immediately, as exploitation appears ongoing.

    The Qilin ransomware gang is exploiting CVE-2026-0257, a critical PAN-OS GlobalProtect authentication bypass flaw, to breach victims’ networks, according to Arctic Wolf. Palo Alto Networks addressed the vulnerability on May 13 and warned that attackers had begun abusing it against unpatched PAN-OS devices without mitigations. Rapid7 had reported seeing exploitation against numerous customers starting on May 17.

    CISA added CVE-2026-0257 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on May 29 and ordered federal agencies to secure their GlobalProtect VPN instances within three days. Arctic Wolf Labs said it investigated multiple June 2026 intrusions that began with exploitation of the flaw and resulted in Qilin ransomware deployment, including domain-wide encryption. The company said post-exploitation activity varied from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion, possibly indicating multiple Qilin affiliates using the same flaw.

    Arctic Wolf assessed with moderate confidence that intrusions using CVE-2026-0257 and leading to Qilin ransomware deployment are likely ongoing. Shadowserver tracks more than 167,000 exposed GlobalProtect VPN instances online, while Shodan found more than 172,000 IPs with a GlobalProtect fingerprint, though the article notes it is unknown how many are patched or honeypots. Qilin is a ransomware-as-a-service operation that surfaced in August 2022 under the name Agenda and has claimed more than 2,000 victims on its leak site.

    • Arctic Wolf observed varied post-exploitation behavior, ranging from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion, which it said may indicate multiple Qilin affiliates are using the same flaw.
    • CISA gave federal agencies only three days to secure affected GlobalProtect instances after adding CVE-2026-0257 to its catalog, underscoring the urgency assigned to this issue.
    • The exposed attack surface is large, with Shadowserver tracking over 167,000 online GlobalProtect VPN instances and Shodan finding over 172,000 IPs with a GlobalProtect fingerprint, though the article notes it is unknown how many are patched or honeypots.
    • Arctic Wolf assessed with moderate confidence that Qilin-related exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is likely ongoing, citing extensive scanning activity and the ransomware-as-a-service model’s tendency to spread successful exploits among affiliates.

In plain words

Attackers linked to Qilin used a recently fixed Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS weakness to get into organizations’ networks without valid sign-in details, then locked files with ransomware. Arctic Wolf Labs saw multiple cases in June 2026 where the attackers moved through Windows systems, stole passwords, erased records of their activity, and sometimes copied data out before locking files. This matters because affected organizations can face both business disruption and possible public exposure or theft of sensitive data.

Summary
Qilin ransomware affiliates are exploiting the patched PAN-OS flaw CVE-2026-0257 to gain unauthorized SSL VPN access and deploy ransomware in victim networks. Attacks commonly involve credential theft, lateral movement with PsExec, Defender disabling, log clearing, and in some cases data exfiltration before encryption.

Threat actors have been observed exploiting the now-patched Palo Alto Networks PAN-OS vulnerability CVE-2026-0257 to deploy Qilin, also known as Agenda, ransomware in victim environments. Arctic Wolf Labs investigated multiple intrusions in June 2026 that began with exploitation of this authentication bypass flaw in the portal and gateway components of PAN-OS. Successful exploitation allowed unauthenticated remote attackers to establish SSL VPN sessions without valid credentials when authentication override cookies were enabled with specific certificate configurations.

After gaining access, the attackers used the VPN sessions to move further into victim networks, harvest credentials, and conduct lateral movement through Windows administrative shares using compromised administrative accounts. Arctic Wolf said the intrusions showed consistent patterns, including staging ransomware at C:\PerfLogs\, using PsExec for lateral execution, deploying password-protected ransomware payloads, clearing logs, and disabling Microsoft Defender Real-Time Protection before running ransomware. The company also noted an unusual Windows Registry persistence pattern involving an asterisk followed by six randomized lowercase alphabetic characters.

The follow-on activity varied across victims, ranging from rapid encryption-only operations to full double-extortion activity. Some cases involved enterprise-wide encryption without data exfiltration and reconnaissance using tools such as AnyDesk, Ngrok, or LogMeIn, while others included large-scale credential theft and data exfiltration to MEGA before ransomware deployment using Rclone, Proton Drive, and FileZilla. Arctic Wolf said this variability is consistent with ransomware-as-a-service models, where multiple affiliates may use shared access infrastructure and ransomware tooling while applying different post-exploitation methods.

  • The same initial access vector led to noticeably different outcomes across victims, which Arctic Wolf said is consistent with multiple Qilin RaaS affiliates using shared access and tooling but applying different post-exploitation methods.

In plain words

Researchers say a group called JADEPUFFER used a flaw in older Langflow software to take over a server and run a new program called ENCFORGE that locks up files used to build and run AI systems. The people most affected are organizations using vulnerable Langflow installations, especially if their AI model files, search indexes, training data, or access keys are reachable from that server. This matters because restoring a damaged AI model could cost tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars and take major engineering work, leaving an organization without a clear path back if its AI assets cannot be recovered.

Summary
Researchers linked JADEPUFFER to a new ENCFORGE ransomware attack that exploits unpatched Langflow RCE to break out via the Docker socket and encrypt AI model files, vector indexes, and training datasets. Organizations should urgently patch Langflow, remove unnecessary Docker socket access, rotate exposed secrets, and keep immutable backups of AI assets.

Researchers at Sysdig linked a second attack on the same Langflow server to JADEPUFFER, the AI-agent-driven operator it documented earlier this month. In the new activity, the operator deployed ENCFORGE, a compiled Go ransomware designed to encrypt AI infrastructure files such as model weights, vector indexes, training datasets, PyTorch and TensorFlow checkpoints, Hugging Face SafeTensors, ONNX files, GGUF files, FAISS indexes, Parquet and Arrow datasets, NumPy arrays, and TensorFlow records. The attack again used CVE-2025-3248, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in Langflow versions before 1.3.0.

Sysdig retrieved the ENCFORGE binary from the attacker’s command-and-control server, where it was hidden as /.lockd. The file is a UPX-packed static Go ELF that uses AES-256-CTR for file data and wraps the per-run key with an embedded RSA-2048 public key. ENCFORGE renames encrypted files with a .locked extension, drops ransom notes, kills processes holding files open, avoids re-encrypting completed files, and deletes itself after running.

After confirming code execution, JADEPUFFER found the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock and adapted when its first attempt to pull ENCFORGE failed. Over five minutes and 24 seconds, the operator created and revised six Python scripts through the Langflow RCE channel until it could create privileged containers, mount the host filesystem, and run ENCFORGE on the host through nsenter. Sysdig found no exfiltration capability in the recovered binary, and the article emphasizes patching Langflow, rotating exposed credentials, removing unnecessary Docker socket access, and keeping offline or immutable snapshots of model files, indexes, and training data.

  • ENCFORGE’s focus on LoRA adapters, GGUF and GGML weights, FAISS indexes, and training datasets shows that the operator is targeting AI recovery capability rather than using a generic file-locking approach.
  • The operator adapted in real time when the initial ENCFORGE download path failed, creating and revising six Python scripts in just over five minutes to reach the host through the exposed Docker socket.
  • The first Python script was built one line at a time and later scripts were base64-decoded inside Python exec calls, showing an effort to avoid simple signature-based detection of complete scripts or shell commands.
  • The shared Proton Mail address between the earlier database-focused campaign and the ENCFORGE ransom notes is described by Sysdig as the strongest attribution link tying the two operations together.
  • Because the recovered ENCFORGE binary had no data theft or leak-site component, immutable or offline backups of model files, vector indexes, and training datasets are especially important for reducing the attacker’s leverage.
Key Points
  • 01Sysdig researchers linked a second attack on the same Langflow server to JADEPUFFER, which deployed a new Go-based ransomware called ENCFORGE.
  • 02The attack used CVE-2025-3248 in Langflow versions before 1.3.0, an unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in the /api/v1/validate/code endpoint.
  • 03ENCFORGE is designed to encrypt AI-related files such as model weights, vector indexes, training datasets, PyTorch and TensorFlow checkpoints, Hugging Face SafeTensors, ONNX files, GGUF files, FAISS indexes, Parquet and Arrow datasets, NumPy arrays, and TensorFlow records.
  • 04JADEPUFFER found the Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock and used it to create privileged containers with host access, then ran ENCFORGE on the host through nsenter.
  • 05Sysdig found no exfiltration capability in the recovered ENCFORGE binary, and the ransom notes used the same Proton Mail address seen in the prior JADEPUFFER campaign.

In plain words

The article describes a critical flaw in a PrestaShop shopping-site feature called ps_facetedsearch, which can let anyone on the internet take control of a store’s server by sending a specially crafted filter value on a normal category page. Public PrestaShop storefronts using ps_facetedsearch versions before 4.0.4 are affected, especially sites with price or weight sliders. This matters because many online stores may have the vulnerable module even if their main PrestaShop software is current, and attackers could use it to place hidden control files on the server and run commands.

Summary
PrestaShop stores using ps_facetedsearch versions 3.0.0 through 4.0.3 are exposed to a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw, CVE-2026-54159, when price or weight slider filters are enabled. Merchants should upgrade the module to version 4.0.4 or later and check for unexpected PHP files or webshell activity.

CVE-2026-54159 is a critical PHP object injection vulnerability in the ps_facetedsearch layered navigation module bundled with PrestaShop. The flaw can let an unauthenticated attacker run arbitrary code on a public storefront and has a CVSS v3.1 base score of 10.0. A visitor-facing category page with a price or weight slider can be enough of an entry point.

The vulnerability affects ps_facetedsearch versions 3.0.0 up to, but not including, 4.0.4. The vulnerable path is reachable when a store runs an affected module version and exposes a price or weight slider filter on front-office pages. The article notes that merchants may keep PrestaShop core current while bundled modules drift behind, leaving older ps_facetedsearch versions exposed.

Technically, the module reads a slider filter value from the request URL without sufficient validation, writes it into a serialized cache, and later processes it with a raw native unserialize() call in src/Filters/Block.php. A crafted value can smuggle a malicious serialized PHP object into the cache, leading to creation of an attacker-controlled PHP file in the module directory that functions as a webshell. PrestaShop has released ps_facetedsearch 4.0.4 to fix the issue by replacing the raw unserialize() call with \Tools::unSerialize(), and defenders are advised to verify module versions, monitor the module directory, and review logs for crafted slider-filter values.

  • A recent PrestaShop core version does not necessarily mean the store is protected, because ps_facetedsearch is a bundled module whose version must be checked directly.
  • The article highlights that exposure often comes from normal storefront features that have worked for years, such as price or weight sliders, making them less likely to receive version checks or configuration review.
  • More than half of the observed exposed assets fell into an unclassified “Others” group, suggesting that affected stores are often secondary, transitional, or poorly inventoried sites rather than only clearly categorized retail properties.
  • The manual fix is only a temporary measure because editing src/Filters/Block.php directly can be undone the next time the module is updated or reinstalled.
Key Points
  • 01CVE-2026-54159 is a critical PHP object injection vulnerability in the PrestaShop ps_facetedsearch module that can allow unauthenticated remote code execution on a storefront.
  • 02The flaw affects ps_facetedsearch versions 3.0.0 up to but not including 4.0.4 when a store exposes a price or weight slider filter on front-office pages.
  • 03The vulnerability occurs because slider filter values from the URL can be written into a serialized cache and later processed by a raw native unserialize() call in src/Filters/Block.php.
  • 04PrestaShop has released ps_facetedsearch version 4.0.4, which fixes the issue by replacing the raw unserialize() call with PrestaShop’s safe \Tools::unSerialize() wrapper.
  • 05Defenders are advised to inventory PrestaShop storefronts, verify installed ps_facetedsearch versions, watch for unexpected PHP files in the module directory, and review logs for crafted slider-filter values.

JUSTIFICATION

This is a must-read because it covers a critical unauthenticated remote code execution flaw in a widely deployed PrestaShop module used on public storefronts. The article identifies affected versions, the exposed configuration, the available fixed version, and concrete actions defenders should take.

In plain words

Researchers found a large operation called FakeGit using 7,600 fake GitHub project pages to trick people into downloading harmful files that can steal information. Many of the pages pretended to be artificial intelligence tools or servers and were even listed in public catalogs, making them easier for developers and AI helpers to find and trust. This matters because GitHub download counters showed more than 14 million download events, though researchers said that number does not mean 14 million infections. Organizations are advised to only use approved tool catalogs, test new tools safely, and change secrets quickly if SmartLoader may have run.

Summary
A large FakeGit campaign is using 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories, including AI tool and MCP server lures, to distribute SmartLoader and StealC malware. Researchers warn that these repos are being surfaced by AI agents and public catalogs, making malicious downloads look more credible to developers.

A large-scale operation called FakeGit is using 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories to distribute SmartLoader and StealC malware. More than 800 of the repositories pretended to be AI skills or MCP servers and appeared more than 600 times in public AI registries and catalogs. Researchers at Island said this increased the chance that AI agents and developers would discover them, a technique they call “agentbaiting.”

The campaign is considered a continuation of an older operation that used Lumma Stealer and was attributed by Trend Micro to a threat actor tracked as Water Kurita. Many repositories imitated consumer and enterprise tools such as Gmail, WhatsApp, Databricks, Jenkins, and Docker, using convincing documentation, fabricated stars and fork counts, copied descriptions, and real developer account names. Their README files directed visitors to ZIP archives that posed as installers or project releases but were disguised Lua payloads that triggered SmartLoader.

Once active, SmartLoader creates persistence through scheduled tasks, retrieves its command-and-control address through a Polygon smart contract, and downloads additional encrypted stages from GitHub before delivering StealC. Island said GitHub public download counters for 335 unique Release assets across 211 FakeGit repositories recorded 14,084,688 cumulative download events, though this included repeated requests and automated activity and should not be interpreted as infections. Island recommends approved catalogs for skills and MCP servers, isolated testing of new capabilities, independent verification of publishers and repositories, and immediate secret rotation where SmartLoader execution is suspected.

  • Public AI registries and catalogs can amplify malicious repositories by making them easier to discover and appear more credible, even when researchers cannot determine whether listings were submitted manually or indexed automatically.
  • In Island’s controlled testing, Claude Code cloned malicious repositories and downloaded malicious files but stopped before execution after detecting suspicious indicators, showing that agent safeguards may intervene late in the workflow rather than at discovery.
  • The campaign’s reported 14,084,688 GitHub download events should be treated as exposure data rather than infection data because the figure includes repeated requests and automated activity.
  • SmartLoader’s use of a Polygon smart contract to retrieve its command-and-control address makes the attack chain depend on infrastructure beyond the malicious GitHub repositories themselves.
  • Island’s recommendation to rotate all secrets immediately where SmartLoader execution is suspected indicates that credential exposure is a primary concern after any successful run.
Key Points
  • 01A campaign called FakeGit is using 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories to distribute SmartLoader and StealC malware.
  • 02More than 800 repositories pretended to be AI skills or MCP servers and appeared over 600 times in public AI registries and catalogs.
  • 03Island researchers said the campaign uses an emerging technique called AgentBaiting to make malicious repositories more visible to AI agents and more likely to be recommended or used.
  • 04The malicious repositories often imitate tools such as Gmail, WhatsApp, Databricks, Jenkins, and Docker, with README files directing users to ZIP archives disguised as installers or releases.
  • 05GitHub public download counters for 335 unique release assets across 211 FakeGit repositories showed 14,084,688 cumulative download events, but Island said this should not be interpreted as infections.

Its scale, supply-chain-style abuse of public developer resources, and actionable defensive recommendations make it highly important for security professionals.

In plain words

A newly revealed Windows problem called LegacyHive can let a regular user on an up-to-date Windows computer change another user’s settings, including an administrator’s, so that unwanted code runs the next time that administrator signs in. It affects Windows 10 version 2004 or later and Windows Server 2022 or later, while Microsoft is still investigating and has not released an official fix. A company called ACROS Security has released free unofficial fixes through its 0Patch tool, because without a fix attackers could use this weakness to get higher control on affected computers.

Summary
Free unofficial 0Patch micropatches are available for the Windows LegacyHive zero-day, which lets non-admin users access another user’s registry hive and potentially gain code execution when an admin logs in. Microsoft is still investigating and has not yet released an official fix.

Free unofficial patches are available for LegacyHive, a recently disclosed Windows zero-day flaw that allows attackers to escalate privileges on up-to-date Windows systems. The vulnerability was found in the Windows User Profile Service by a researcher using the handle Nightmare Eclipse and was disclosed on the day Microsoft released its July 2026 Patch Tuesday updates. Microsoft has not yet assigned a CVE ID or released official security updates for the issue, and said it is aware of the report and actively investigating the claims.

After analyzing the proof-of-concept exploit, Tharros principal vulnerability analyst Will Dormann said non-admin users can exploit LegacyHive to modify the classes registry hive and gain automatic code execution when an admin account logs into a compromised device. ACROS Security, the company behind the 0Patch platform, said the vulnerability allows a regular non-admin user to mount any other user’s registry hive in full access mode and either extract stored secrets or change registry values that affect what runs at the next login. Kevin Beaumont confirmed that the exploit works and published Microsoft Defender for Endpoint detection queries for LegacyHive.

ACROS Security is providing free 0Patch micropatches for Windows 10 2004 or later and Windows Server 2022 or later, because the flaw does not affect systems older than Windows 10 2004 and Windows Server 2019. The company said that with 0Patch enabled, the exploit appears to work but loads a temporary user profile hive instead of the targeted admin user’s hive, which is of no use to the attacker. The micropatch can be deployed through the 0Patch agent without requiring a system restart unless custom patching policies block it.

In plain words

Kaspersky found a new part of the Project CAV3RN spying toolset that hides instructions and stolen results inside Outlook calendar events in a compromised Microsoft 365 mailbox belonging to an Israeli law firm. If its Microsoft access stops working, the tool can ask an attacker-controlled internet address for replacement settings so it can keep communicating. This matters because it shows the group is actively improving its tools and using ordinary cloud services in ways that can make spying activity harder to notice.

Summary
Kaspersky analyzed a new Project CAV3RN communication module that uses Microsoft Graph to hide command-and-control traffic in Outlook calendar events, with encrypted attachments carrying commands and results. If Microsoft Graph access fails, the module can recover replacement Microsoft 365 connection settings through attacker-controlled DNS AAAA records.

Kaspersky analyzed a newly identified Project CAV3RN communication module named AzureCommunication.dll, a .NET Native AOT DLL that appears designed to replace the framework’s earlier HTTP/WebSocket communication component. The module exchanges commands, heartbeats, and command results through Outlook calendar events accessed via Microsoft Graph. The default configuration includes Microsoft Entra tenant details, application credentials, a target mailbox, a DNS bootstrap host, and RSA keys used for communication.

The module uses the default calendar of the configured mailbox as a dead-drop channel, placing activity in a fixed one-hour window on May 13, 2050. Operator commands are stored in events with subjects containing Event ID: <agent-id>, while heartbeats and results use Boss update ID: <agent-id>1500 and Boss Report ID: <agent-id>1500. Commands and results are carried as encrypted attachments, using RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 to protect an AES-256-GCM key.

If Microsoft Graph authentication or validation fails, the module attempts to recover replacement TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, and UserEmail values through DNS AAAA responses from cloudlanecdn[.]com. The DNS recovery protocol embeds the agent ID in queries and treats returned IPv6 addresses as containers for configuration data rather than network destinations. Kaspersky retains a low-confidence assessment that Project CAV3RN is associated with OilRig, citing behavioral similarities such as use of Microsoft-hosted services and a secondary mechanism for restoring access to a cloud command-and-control channel.

  • All command, heartbeat, and result events use the same fixed one-hour calendar window in 2050, making that specific future time range a concrete hunting location for suspicious Outlook calendar activity.
  • The module leaves a local configuration artifact named logAzure.txt in the current working directory, containing Microsoft Graph connection settings and RSA keys used by the communication channel.
  • Command and result attachments differ by filename capitalization, with operator-to-agent commands using file0.txt and agent-to-operator results using File0.txt.
  • The DNS recovery mechanism only updates TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, and UserEmail, but not the recovery domain or RSA keys, limiting what the operators can rotate through DNS alone.
  • The domain cloudlanecdn.com shifted from Namecheap-managed nameservers to custom in-bailiwick authoritative nameservers on May 2, 2026, aligning with the module’s need for actor-controlled DNS responses.
Key Points
  • 01Kaspersky identified a .NET Native AOT communication module named AzureCommunication.dll that appears designed to replace Project CAV3RN’s earlier HTTP/WebSocket communication component.
  • 02The module exchanges commands, heartbeats, and command results through Outlook calendar events accessed via Microsoft Graph in the default calendar of a configured Microsoft 365 mailbox.
  • 03Commands and results are stored as encrypted calendar event attachments, using RSA-OAEP with SHA-256 to protect an AES-256-GCM key.
  • 04If Microsoft Graph authentication or tenant validation fails, the module attempts to recover replacement TenantId, ClientId, ClientSecret, and UserEmail values through DNS AAAA responses from cloudlanecdn.com.
  • 05Kaspersky retains a low-confidence assessment that Project CAV3RN is associated with OilRig based on behavioral similarities, including use of Microsoft-hosted services and a secondary recovery mechanism for cloud command-and-control access.

In plain words

Researchers tested five open-source Android phone-control AI tools and found that all were fooled by hidden or altered text on the phone screen, with some cases letting a malicious Android app make the computer running the tool execute commands. This mainly affects people using these developer tools with Android debugging enabled, not ordinary phones with built-in assistants. It matters because the setup instructions for some of these tools create much of the risk by trusting what the AI sees on the screen and by sending phone input through channels that other apps can watch or abuse.

Summary
Researchers found that five open-source Android AI agent frameworks can be manipulated by hidden or tampered screen text to leak input, spoof actions, and in some cases execute commands on the host PC via unsafe ADB shell handling. The core takeaway is that these agents treat model-perceived screen content as trusted input, but the LLM and screenshot pipeline are not security boundaries.

Researchers demonstrated seven attacks against five open-source mobile agent frameworks: AppAgent, AppAgentX, Mobile-Agent-v3, Open-AutoGLM, and MobA. Every framework fell to at least six of the seven attacks, according to a paper posted on arXiv on July 1 and revised on July 14. The attacks show that an Android app with abilities such as drawing over other windows or writing to shared storage can feed hidden instructions to the AI agent controlling the phone.

The most serious chain described in the article can move from invisible or tampered screen text to commands running on the PC that is driving the agent. AppAgent’s controller is highlighted because it uses a shell call and builds ADB text input from model output with inadequate filtering, leaving shell metacharacters able to affect the host shell. The researchers also found screenshot race conditions, broadcast-based input exposure, fake login screens, and hidden text in low-opacity screen regions or phone corner cutouts.

The article says there are no CVEs and that the researchers have no evidence of the techniques being used outside a controlled setting. The affected software is open-source developer tooling, not built-in phone assistants, and the preconditions include an installed app, an agent mid-task, and USB or wireless debugging enabled. Suggested fixes include dropping shell=True, streaming screenshots instead of writing them to device storage, protecting input broadcasts, checking foreground app changes, and applying contrast enhancement, though the paper says some hardware-related hidden-screen issues have no straightforward software fix.

  • The article highlights that model-visible text can be effectively invisible to humans, since all six tested vision models read 2%-opacity text in at least 18 of 20 trials while the paper describes that level as below typical human detection under normal viewing.
  • A security prompt is not a reliable fallback in these systems because Open-AutoGLM’s prompt only appears when the model judges an action to be sensitive, and perception attacks can alter that judgment before the prompt is triggered.
  • Some safer implementation choices already exist across the tested projects, but no project combines them: MobA avoids the screenshot file race by streaming screenshots, while Open-AutoGLM avoids host command injection by passing arguments as lists.
  • The phone’s physical shape creates a software-visible blind spot, because pixels hidden under rounded corners or camera cutouts still appear in screenshots and were read by all five agents in the researchers’ tests.
  • The article identifies a disclosure gap around research-grade open-source AI agent projects, noting that none of the five repositories had a published security policy and the researchers had not received responses from maintainers.
Key Points
  • 01Researchers demonstrated seven attacks against five open-source mobile agent frameworks: AppAgent, AppAgentX, Mobile-Agent-v3, Open-AutoGLM, and MobA, and every framework was vulnerable to at least six of the seven attacks.
  • 02The paper describes a chain in which an Android app that can draw over other windows and write to shared storage can place invisible instructions for the AI agent, and in some cases those instructions can lead to commands running on the PC controlling the agent.
  • 03AppAgent’s controller builds ADB shell text input from model output with insufficient sanitization, leaving shell metacharacters such as semicolons and ampersands able to be interpreted by the host shell.
  • 04The researchers found screenshot race conditions in several frameworks because screenshots were written to shared device storage before being pulled, giving a malicious background service a 50 to 500 millisecond window to alter the image.
  • 05The article says the researchers privately emailed affected maintainers before posting the preprint but had not received a response, and The Hacker News found no published security policy in any of the five repositories.

This is a specific research finding affecting five named open-source Android AI agent frameworks, with demonstrated paths from hidden screen content to input leakage, UI spoofing, screenshot tampering, and host command execution. There is no evidence of exploitation in the wild and no CVEs, but the findings are broadly relevant because the affected tools document setup steps that create many of the required preconditions.

Researchers at Zhejiang University described Bit2Watt, a technique in which a cloud tenant with ordinary GPU access could make a data center’s power draw rise and fall rapidly without using an exploit or breaking into control systems. The paper, accepted to CHES 2026, combines measurements on real GPUs with simulations of possible grid destabilization. The article emphasizes that the work does not disclose a flaw in a specific commercial product and that no production systems were attacked.

Bit2Watt works by making GPU power use follow controlled changes in computation, switching between high-intensity activity and near-idle states. The researchers tested SWMA, a purpose-built CUDA kernel, and LTMA, which hides modulation inside an LLM training run through hyperparameter changes and auxiliary operations. LTMA runs at lower frequencies than SWMA but produces larger amplitude and blends more easily into normal training noise, making it harder to flag.

The most severe grid impacts came from simulations, including a worst-case 1 MW local grid with 1,000 GPUs modulating in perfect lockstep and a larger 9,241-bus grid model. The article notes that a real attack would require enough physically clustered GPUs, tight synchronization, power modulation that survives data-center power conditioning, and a grid resonance that amplifies the chosen frequency. It also describes related risks, including GPU servers shutting down from heat or overcurrent protection, a near-field electromagnetic covert channel, and the lack of conventional monitoring that can easily observe modulation running above common telemetry sampling rates.

  • The most concerning version of Bit2Watt is not the custom CUDA kernel but the LLM-training variant, because it produces larger power swings while blending into normal training activity and is harder for operators to flag.
  • Existing data-center telemetry may miss the relevant behavior because common power and GPU monitoring interfaces sample at or below about 1 kHz, while the demonstrated modulation can run several times faster.
  • The attack surface sits between organizations that usually operate separately: cloud providers monitor compute workloads, while utilities monitor grid behavior, and the article says neither side is built to watch the other.
  • The paper’s strongest grid-damage results depend on an optimistic attacker assumption: many GPUs must switch in close lockstep, and the article notes that even 100 microseconds of timing jitter reduced aggregate amplitude by about 20% in the model.
  • The risk is not purely theoretical because Microsoft, OpenAI, and NVIDIA previously warned that synchronized AI-training power swings can cause physical grid damage when they align with critical utility frequencies.
Key Points
  • 01Zhejiang University researchers described Bit2Watt, a technique in which a cloud tenant uses ordinary GPU access to rapidly modulate a data center’s power draw without exploiting a software flaw or breaking into control systems.
  • 02The researchers tested two methods: SWMA, a purpose-built CUDA kernel that switches between high-intensity and near-idle states, and LTMA, which hides similar modulation inside an LLM training run.
  • 03In the paper’s worst-case simulation of a 1 MW local grid with 1,000 synchronized GPUs, current total harmonic distortion reached 46.8% and the damping ratio fell to -0.27, indicating an unstable mode in the model.
  • 04The article states that a real attack would require several conditions to align, including enough physically clustered GPUs, tight synchronization, power modulation that survives data-center power conditioning, and a grid resonance that amplifies the chosen frequency.
  • 05The researchers also described Watt2Bit feedback effects that could trip GPU server protections and a near-field electromagnetic covert channel that recovered a 50-bit test sequence with zero errors.

Researchers found a fake NuGet software package called Newtonsoftt.Json.Net that looked like the popular Newtonsoft.Json library and still worked like a normal JSON tool, but secretly targeted Digitain’s BetOnGames FG-Crash betting game. Summary
JFrog found a typosquatted NuGet package, Newtonsoftt.Json.Net, that impersonated Newtonsoft.Json while secretly targeting Digitain’s FG-Crash betting platform to rig game results and, in later versions, exfiltrate them to an attacker-controlled server. The key takeaway is that a supply-chain package can appear fully functional and harmless to most users while carrying a highly targeted payload for one specific victim.

JFrog Security Research discovered and disclosed a typosquatted NuGet package named Newtonsoftt.Json.Net, which masqueraded as the popular Newtonsoft.Json library while shipping a trojanized fork. The package specifically targeted Digitain’s BetOnGames FG-Crash betting game and, in later versions, exfiltrated rigged round results to an attacker-controlled server using the header X-Seq-ApiKey: theperfectheist2025. The package was available and discoverable from August 2025 to October 2025, and although it was later unlisted, the article states that its artifacts remained available for download at the time of writing.

The malicious package was notable because it worked as a functional JSON library for users who installed it, while its harmful behavior only activated in a specific environment. The trigger was tied to the JsonConvert.DefaultSettings property setter, after which the payload used HarmonyLib to patch Digitain.FG.SharedCrash.GameLogic.SharedCrashRules.GenerateGameResult following a delay. Across seven versions, the package evolved through three generations, moving from local-only rigging to versions with exfiltration and then to a cleaner postfix-based method of overwriting game results.

The impact described in the article is targeted financial fraud against Digitain’s crash-style betting platform, with the attacker gaining prior knowledge and partial control of crash multipliers on a schedule only they knew. Gen-2 and Gen-3 variants also sent rigged results to hxxp[:]//185[.]126[.]237[.]64:5341/api/events/raw in traffic designed to resemble Seq structured logging. JFrog disclosed the issue to Digitain on July 7, 2026, and Digitain responded on July 9, 2026, that it was already aware of the reported issue and had resolved it.

  • The malicious package was designed to remain invisible to most users because it functioned as a real JSON library and only became harmful on systems exposing Digitain’s specific FG-Crash backend method.
  • The package metadata itself exposed the intended victim by repeatedly including an internal Digitain TFS repository URL for the BetOnGames FG-Crash project.
  • The attacker used delayed activation, including a 10-minute delay in Gen-3 and a next-day timing pattern in Gen-1, to move the malicious behavior away from application startup when operators were less likely to notice it.
  • The exfiltration traffic was shaped to look like normal Seq structured logging, using the same raw ingest path, header style, and event format to blend in with application telemetry.
  • The unobfuscated 11.0.11 release made the C2 URL, API key, and message template recoverable directly from the binary, unlike earlier ConfuserEx-protected versions.

Attackers in Colombia and Mexico abused exposed or misconfigured RDP and MSSQL services, then used legitimate tools like BitLocker and RMM software to encrypt systems and print ransom notes from office printers. The key lesson is that poor configuration, disabled protection, and ignored alerts can let intruders turn built-in enterprise tools into low-cost ransomware infrastructure.

Kaspersky teams in Latin America investigated incidents in Colombia and Mexico involving misconfiguration, BitLocker encryption, and corporate printers used to deliver ransom notes. In both cases, affected users first saw locked drives in Windows Explorer and were prompted for BitLocker recovery keys. The article says these attacks show adversaries gaining infrastructure access while avoiding investment in or partnership with ransomware groups by using built-in Microsoft tools for encryption.

In the Colombia case, attackers exploited an internet-exposed RDP service on a machine connected to an 8 TB storage device containing mission-critical data. They manipulated user credentials, enabled BitLocker on the drive that primarily stored financial data, and printed ransom notes after encryption was complete. The attackers demanded $3,000, but the company restored the system before forensic investigators could collect evidence, eliminating information needed to assess the incident.

In the Mexico case, attackers exploited a misconfigured Microsoft SQL Server service after obtaining database login credentials from code insecurely published on GitHub. The server allowed operating system command execution through the xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure, and the attackers later deployed RMM tools including ManageEngine Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, and Tactical RMM. They used scheduled tasks and a Group Policy Object to enable BitLocker encryption across systems, after which users saw “Hacked by XEntry Team” and ransom notes emerged from office printers.

Summary
Microsoft says WSUS sync delays and timeouts caused by excess publishing metadata have been mitigated for new or rebuilt servers, but existing affected WSUS installations may need manual cleanup. Microsoft shared manual mitigations for Windows Server Update Services servers affected by a known issue that causes Windows Update scans to fail or time out. The issue affects Windows 10, version 1607 and later, and Windows Server 2012 and later. On impacted WSUS servers, administrators may be unable to deploy the latest Windows updates through WSUS or Configuration Manager because synchronization takes longer or times out.

Microsoft said the delays were caused by a buildup of publishing metadata, and it rolled out a service-side mitigation for newly installed or rebuilt WSUS servers. The company said synchronization times and sync operations have been restored and are operating normally for new WSUS installations and rebuilds. For existing WSUS installations that still have long sync times, Microsoft said organizations can clean up unneeded metadata that is present but safe to remove.

Microsoft’s manual steps include backing up each SUSDB database, running a cleanup query from SQL Management Studio against all SUSDB databases including WSUS replicas, and updating MaxXMLPerRequest to its default setting. After cleanup, administrators should reindex SUSDB, run the WSUS Server Cleanup Wizard, and reset IIS or recycle the WsusPool application pool to clear cached catalog state. Microsoft said the first Windows Update scan after cleanup may take longer than usual, but later scans should return to normal timing.

  • Microsoft’s service-side mitigation only restores normal synchronization for newly installed or rebuilt WSUS servers, so existing affected installations still require manual database cleanup.
  • The metadata causing the delays is described by Microsoft as safe to remove, which makes the recommended cleanup a supported remediation rather than a workaround that changes update content.
  • Administrators should include WSUS replicas when running the SUSDB cleanup query, not just primary WSUS databases.
  • Microsoft notes that the first Windows Update scan after cleanup may still be slower than usual, so normal performance should be judged by subsequent scans.
  • The client-side DataStore.edb file is not expected to shrink after the metadata is removed, and Microsoft says this does not affect scan performance.

Researchers found that AWS Kiro could be tricked by hidden instructions on a web page into rewriting its MCP configuration and running attacker-controlled code on a developer’s machine without meaningful approval. AWS has patched the flaw by protecting sensitive configuration paths, and users should update to current Kiro versions.

Intezer, in research with Kodem Security, found that hidden text on a web page could make AWS Kiro rewrite its own configuration file and run attacker-controlled code on a developer’s machine. The attack could start from an ordinary request, such as asking Kiro to summarize a page, and did not give the developer a meaningful approval step before code execution. AWS has patched the issue, and no CVE has been assigned.

The flaw centered on Kiro’s ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json file, which listed Model Context Protocol servers and the commands used to start them. At the time of the research, Kiro could write to that file with its fsWrite tool without approval and automatically reload it, launching whatever command the modified file described with the developer’s privileges. Intezer’s proof of concept placed instructions in one-pixel white text on an API documentation page, and the demo payload only sent the machine’s hostname, username, and platform to prove execution.

AWS fixed the issue by marking mcp.json, .vscode/tasks.json, the .git directory, and other sensitive files as protected paths requiring explicit approval before writes. Intezer confirmed the attack failed in Kiro v0.11.130, and current builds are on the 1.0.x line, with 1.0.165 listed as latest as of July 21, 2026. The article notes that earlier Kiro issues had a similar pattern: an agent quietly editing files that decide what it is allowed to execute.

  • Kiro’s approval pop-up did not provide real protection in some cases because the MCP configuration reloaded regardless of whether the developer approved the change.
  • The same class of issue had appeared in Kiro before, but AWS’s earlier fix applied only to Supervised mode while the default Autopilot mode could still write the sensitive file on its own.
  • Intezer said the attack was not perfectly reliable because the model might summarize the page and ignore the hidden instructions, but it still worked within one or two tries in testing.
  • AWS’s later protected-paths fix is notable because it applies in both Autopilot and Supervised mode, unlike the earlier 2025 mitigation.
  • The article highlights Kiro’s own documentation stating that Supervised mode is a code review workflow, not a security control, reinforcing that enforcement must happen outside the model’s decision-making.
Key Points
  • 01Intezer, working with Kodem Security, found that hidden text on a web page could cause AWS Kiro to rewrite its own MCP configuration file and run attacker-controlled code on a developer’s machine.
  • 02The flaw involved Kiro’s ability to write to ~/.kiro/settings/mcp.json without approval and then automatically reload it, launching whatever external tool command the file described with the developer’s privileges.
  • 03Intezer’s proof of concept used one-pixel white text on an API documentation page, and the payload only sent the machine’s hostname, username, and platform to prove code execution.
  • 04AWS patched the issue by marking mcp.json, .vscode/tasks.json, the .git directory, and other sensitive files as protected paths that require explicit approval before writes.
  • 05No CVE has been assigned to this finding, and Intezer reported no in-the-wild exploitation.

Summary
A phishing email hid a fake Disney+ credential-harvesting page behind a redirect chain that started with Google, passed through an is.gd short link, and ended on Azure Front Door infrastructure. The key lesson is that URL defenses must follow every redirect to the final rendered page instead of trusting the reputation of intermediate platforms.

A phishing email reached an HR business partner at a hospitality company with almost no content except a single link that appeared to begin with https://www.google.com/. The subject line was padded with invisible spacing and included C A L L E R R e f : # followed by a GUID. Although the visible link used Google’s redirect endpoint, the click path ultimately led to a Disney+-branded credential-harvesting page.

The redirect chain moved from google.com/url?q=... to an is.gd short link and then to a Microsoft Azure Front Door subdomain on azurefd.net. The article says this structure laundered trust through services that security teams would hesitate to block wholesale, including Google, is.gd, and Microsoft infrastructure. Reputation-based URL filtering could treat each visible or intermediate domain as safe unless it expanded every hop to the final destination.

The message was not cleanly authenticated, because DKIM failed and Microsoft scored it as spam with SCL:5, SFV:SPM, and category SPM. The sender domain ocean-pacific[.]net was new to the organization, and the sending IP was in Singapore with a helo of [127.0.0.1]. IRONSCALES link analysis followed the full redirect chain, identified the terminal page as credential harvesting, and later observed that the same host returned a CAPTCHA instead of the Disney+ login prompt on re-scan.

  • The article emphasizes that the phishing email did not succeed because it passed authentication checks; DKIM failed and Microsoft scored it as spam, so the real weakness was link analysis that trusted intermediate domains.
  • The attacker used infrastructure that defenders would hesitate to block wholesale, including Google redirects, is.gd, and Azure Front Door, making platform reputation a poor indicator of safety.
  • The final phishing page was not consistently visible, because a later scan returned a CAPTCHA instead of the Disney+-branded login prompt, showing why one-time or automated checks can miss the actual lure.
  • The combination of a first-time sender, failed DKIM, empty body, unusual subject formatting, and a single Google-wrapped link created a stronger phishing signal than any individual domain in the redirect chain.

The Senate Intelligence Committee voted 9-8 along party lines to support President Donald Trump’s nominee for director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton. The vote clears an important hurdle and allows the full Senate to decide whether Clayton should be confirmed as the country’s latest spy chief. That vote is likely to happen before senators leave for their August recess.

Committee Democrats raised concerns during Clayton’s confirmation hearing that he could politicize the position on Trump’s behalf. Those concerns followed Clayton’s refusal to acknowledge that Joe Biden defeated Trump in the 2020 election, saying only that Biden was “certified.” Clayton was also questioned about former director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard’s visit to a Georgia election office during an FBI search related to the 2020 election.

Clayton’s confirmation could potentially clear the way for bipartisan legislation to renew Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act. The law allows the National Security Agency to collect certain foreign intelligence from international phone calls and emails involving hackers, foreign spies and other perceived overseas security threats, but it also intercepts Americans’ data. The statute expired last month after Democrats said they would not support the bill while acting intelligence director Bill Pulte remained in office.

The article argues organizations should continuously validate whether vulnerabilities are actually exploitable in their environment and whether controls can stop them, rather than relying only on severity scores and faster patching.

The article argues that N-day exploitation is becoming an “N-hour” problem because AI can now turn software patches into working exploits far faster than defenders can deploy fixes. It cites Anthropic red team research in which Claude Mythos Preview converted 18 Firefox patches into 8 working code-execution exploits, with the first appearing in under an hour after Mozilla shipped the patch. It also describes Windows kernel testing where the model built proof-of-concept crashes for 18 of 21 bugs and chained 8 to SYSTEM using stripped binaries and decompiler output.

The article says the old patch-first playbook is breaking because the patch that protects updated systems also reveals what was broken to attackers. It cites Verizon’s 2026 DBIR reporting a 43-day median time to fix known-exploited flaws and Zero Day Clock data showing 2026’s average time-to-exploit at less than 24 hours. Because patches often wait on regression testing, change windows, and uptime commitments, the article argues defenders should ask which exposures can actually be exploited in their environment and whether controls would stop the attempt.

It describes three methods: safely firing real exploit chains where possible, decomposing exploits into attacker behaviors and testing each link against controls where live exploitation is unsafe, and continuously checking live security tools against new attacker techniques. In plain words

Kenya is investigating an incident where the president’s official website was briefly taken over and replaced with an anti-government message demanding about $330,000 in bitcoin. The affected party is the Kenyan government, especially the office of President William Ruto, but officials say the site has been restored and they have not found evidence that sensitive information was stolen or leaked. It matters because government websites are public sources of information and trust, and this follows earlier disruptions of several Kenyan government websites.

Summary
Kenya is investigating a hack that briefly defaced President William Ruto’s official website with an anti-government message demanding five bitcoins. Officials say the site has been restored and there is no evidence sensitive data was accessed or leaked.

Kenya is investigating a cyberattack that temporarily defaced President William Ruto’s official website. The homepage was replaced on Saturday with an anti-government message demanding five bitcoins, worth about $330,000. The message displayed a cryptocurrency wallet address and threatened to publish unspecified information about the president unless the ransom was paid.

By Monday, access to the website had been restored, according to local media. Information, Communications and the Digital Economy Cabinet Secretary William Kabogo confirmed the cyberattack and said government cybersecurity teams were investigating. He said access to the presidential website was temporarily restricted to support containment, forensic analysis, and restoration.

Kabogo said authorities found no evidence of unauthorized access to sensitive data, data exfiltration, or loss of information, and that government systems and digital services remained secure and operational. Screenshots shared on social media showed the attackers claiming the message was their “third” warning, but authorities have not confirmed that claim and no verified data leak has been made public. The incident follows a November 2025 coordinated cyberattack that temporarily disrupted multiple Kenyan government websites, including the presidency and several ministries.

  • The ransom demand was paired with a threat to publish information, but authorities said they found no evidence of sensitive data access, exfiltration, or information loss.
  • The attackers’ claim that this was their “third” warning has not been confirmed, and no verified data leak has been made public.
  • Kenyan authorities temporarily restricted access to the presidential website specifically to support containment, forensic analysis, and restoration.
  • The presidency’s website has now been named in multiple cyber incidents, including this defacement and a coordinated disruption of Kenyan government websites in November 2025.

The attacker then creates the Chef extension on a Windows or Linux Azure VM with settings that point to the rogue Chef server and run the malicious recipe.

The article highlights that several built-in Azure roles have the required extension write permission, including Owner, Contributor, Log Analytics Contributor, and Virtual Machine Contributor, as well as several less commonly used roles. Summary
Tyro CISO Arun Singh argues that security teams can’t scale effective controls unless developers trust them, because clumsy rollouts can make future nuanced policies harder to adopt. He recommends low-friction tools embedded in developer workflows, such as IDE scanning and device protection, to improve security without disrupting productivity.

The article is based on a conversation with Arun Singh, who has led security for major Australian fintechs and says technical skill alone is not enough if security leaders cannot influence the business. He describes an early decision to remove local administrator rights across every workstation, which worked for most users but severely hurt the productivity of software engineers who needed deeper system access. Although his team found a compromise within days, he says trust with those engineers took about a year to rebuild.

Singh says Tyro’s recent board conversations have focused on supply chain attacks, where long-standing advice to keep packages and dependencies up to date can create new problems. His team now advocates a 7-day cooldown period for new package versions, which means asking developers to delay some updates rather than apply them immediately. The article says this kind of nuanced policy only works if developers trust the security team enough to follow it instead of ignoring or working around it.

The article argues that developer trust is a finite resource and that security teams should choose tools and rollout strategies that avoid unnecessary friction. Singh prioritizes in-IDE vulnerability detection so insecure code patterns, secrets, and vulnerabilities can be caught while engineers are still working. He also points to developer device protection that can enforce policies by blocking malicious packages, browser extensions, and IDE plugins at install time without disrupting safe activity.

  • A security control can technically succeed for most employees while still failing strategically if it disrupts a small but critical developer group and damages trust for future rollouts.
  • Supply chain defense may require reversing years of security messaging, because the article says attackers have used the push to rapidly update packages as a way to compromise companies.
  • A nuanced policy such as waiting seven days before adopting new package versions depends less on enforcement alone and more on whether engineers believe the security team’s reasoning.
  • The article frames developer trust as a limited resource that security teams should deliberately preserve when choosing tools and rollout strategies.
